01.note: A borrower told his lender: whenever you say I have not repaid, I will believe you as if you were two witnesses. He then repaid the loan in front of three witnesses. Rav Pappa ruled that the lender could not deny it: the borrower had trusted him like two witnesses, not like three. Rav Huna, son of Rav Yehoshua, objected that following the larger number applies to estimates of value, where more people know more, but in testimony a hundred witnesses are like two and two are like a hundred.
01.why: The Gemara has just argued over a borrower who makes his lender believable against any claim of repayment, and whether that trust can outweigh witnesses; this case asks whether the number of witnesses changes the answer.

people.name: Rav Pappa
people.about: The Sage who rules that trust 'like two witnesses' does not stand against three.

people.name: Rav Huna, son of Rav Yehoshua
people.about: The Sage who objects that in testimony the number of witnesses beyond two makes no difference.

terms.meaning: The rule that when people disagree, the view held by more of them is accepted. Rav Huna says it fits estimates of value, not testimony.

02.note: The Romans arrested Rabbi Elazar ben Perata on five charges and Rabbi Hanina ben Teradyon on one. Hanina told Elazar he would be saved, because he had done acts of kindness as well as study Torah, while Hanina would not. At his trial Elazar denied teaching Torah and stealing, and miracles backed him: hornets showed which wool was warp and which woof, and an old man was trampled at the house of Abidan that day, as he said he feared. When a man rose to testify that he had freed his slave, Elijah flung a letter the man carried four hundred parasangs, and the man went after it and never came back. Hanina, asked why he taught Torah, said 'As the Lord my God commanded me.' He was sentenced to burning, his wife to execution, his daughter to a brothel.
02.why: The Gemara returns to the Sages tried by the Romans. Along the way it uses Hanina's words to teach, with Rav Huna, that Torah study without acts of kindness is not enough, and it explains what each of the three had done to deserve their sentence.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar ben Perata
people.about: A Sage arrested by the Romans on five charges, who is saved through a series of miracles.

people.name: Rabbi Hanina ben Teradyon
people.about: A Sage arrested for teaching Torah in public, sentenced to burning; the Gemara says he pronounced God's name in public.

people.name: Elijah
people.about: The prophet, who appears disguised as a Roman nobleman to stop a witness against Rabbi Elazar ben Perata.

terms.meaning: The two sets of threads in weaving: the warp is stretched on the loom and the woof is passed through it. An expert weaver can tell them apart.
A meeting place where debates on wisdom and faith were held, which the Romans expected Rabbi Elazar ben Perata to attend.
God's proper name, which by tradition is not pronounced as it is written.
A Persian measure of distance, roughly four kilometers; four hundred of them is a very great distance.

03.note: Rabbi Yehuda Nesia was walking, leaning on the shoulder of his attendant Rabbi Simlai, and told him: you missed the study hall last night, when we permitted the oil of gentiles. Simlai replied that in their days he would permit gentiles' bread as well. Rabbi Yehuda Nesia answered that people would then call them a permissive court, as they had called Rabbi Yosei ben Yo'ezer 'Yosef the Permissive' for his three lenient rulings. Simlai pointed out that Yosei had permitted three things, Rabbi Yehuda Nesia only one, so another would make just two. Rabbi Yehuda Nesia said he had already permitted another: according to Shmuel, it was his court that allowed a woman to remarry under a certain conditional bill of divorce.
03.why: The exchange is the Gemara's record that Rabbi Yehuda Nesia's court permitted gentiles' oil; the Gemara then turns aside to examine that same court's ruling on the conditional bill of divorce.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda Nesia
people.about: The head of the court that permitted the oil of gentiles.

people.name: Rabbi Simlai
people.about: Rabbi Yehuda Nesia's attendant, who was absent from the study hall the night the oil was permitted.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei ben Yo'ezer of Tzereida
people.about: An earlier Sage nicknamed 'Yosef the Permissive' for three lenient rulings.

terms.meaning: Olive oil made by non-Jews, which had been forbidden to Jews until this court permitted it.
The document a husband gives his wife to end a marriage. Here it was given on a condition, and the husband died before the condition could be tested.
The early collection of rabbinic teachings on which the Gemara comments.

04.note: Rav Ashi came to a certain place where he was served a fish that looked like a shefarnuna. He put it in a white vessel, saw the scales it shed, and permitted it. Rabba bar bar Hana came to Akra DeAgma and was served tzahanta, a dish of small fish, and heard a man call it batei, the name of a non-kosher sea creature. He concluded there was something non-kosher in it and did not eat. In the morning he examined the dish, found a non-kosher substance in it, and applied to himself the verse: 'No sin shall befall the righteous.'
04.why: The Gemara is gathering cases of Sages deciding whether an unfamiliar fish was kosher, mostly by looking for scales; Rabba bar bar Hana's case adds a different kind of evidence, a name overheard at the table.

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: A Sage who checks a doubtful fish for scales and permits it.

people.name: Rabba bar bar Hana
people.about: A Sage who refuses a dish because of what a man called it, and turns out to be right.

terms.meaning: A fish is kosher only if it has fins and scales, so finding scales settles whether a doubtful fish may be eaten.
A kind of fish the Gemara has just called permitted.
Food that Jewish law forbids to be eaten.

05.note: Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda taught that one may not make even a wooden candelabrum like the Temple's, as the Hasmoneans made one of wood. The Rabbis answered that the Hasmoneans' candelabrum was not wood: its branches were iron spits covered with tin. When they grew richer they made it of silver, and when they grew richer still, of gold.
05.why: Abaye cites this teaching for his view that the Torah bans making only copies that can truly reproduce their model, such as a seven-branched candelabrum, which is why figures of the moon were allowed.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda
people.about: A Sage who holds that even a wooden copy of the Temple candelabrum is forbidden.

terms.meaning: The seven-branched lampstand (menorah) that stood in the Temple. A private copy with seven lamps is forbidden.
The family of priests who ruled Judea and purified the Temple; the text says they first had to make the candelabrum from poor materials.
A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna.

06.note: Rav taught that if the altar was damaged, all offerings slaughtered there are disqualified, adding that there was a verse for this but they had forgotten which. When his disciple Rav Kahana went up to the Land of Israel, he heard Rabbi Shimon, son of Rabbi, teach in the name of Rabbi Yishmael, son of Rabbi Yosei, that the source is 'You shall slaughter upon it your burnt offerings and your peace offerings': offerings are slaughtered on account of the altar when it is whole, not when it is damaged. Rav Kahana said: this is the verse that eluded Rav.
06.why: Rav's rule opens a new topic on the damaged altar; the Gemara goes on to set it against Rabbi Yohanan, who says that even animals not yet slaughtered when the altar was damaged are disqualified.

people.name: Rav
people.about: A Sage who knew the ruling on a damaged altar but had forgotten its source verse.

people.name: Rav Kahana
people.about: Rav's disciple, who finds the missing verse in the Land of Israel.

people.name: Rabbi Shimon, son of Rabbi
people.about: The Sage whom Rav Kahana heard teaching the verse.

people.name: Rabbi Yishmael, son of Rabbi Yosei
people.about: The Sage in whose name the verse was taught.

terms.meaning: Unfit to be offered, so the sacrifice does not count.
Two kinds of animal sacrifice: a burnt offering is burned whole on the altar, and most of a peace offering is eaten by its owners.

07.note: In another version of the incident, Ravina told Mar bar Rav Ashi, at the very place where it happened, that the corner of his garment had torn. Mar bar Rav Ashi answered: do you think I should throw it off? Doesn't the Master say that human dignity is so great that it overrides a prohibition of the Torah?
07.why: The Gemara is asking how a Sage could keep wearing a garment he was not allowed to carry. In this version he knew and relied on human dignity, and the Gemara explains that this works because the place was a karmelit, where carrying is forbidden only by rabbinic law.

people.name: Ravina
people.about: The Sage who tells Mar bar Rav Ashi that his garment has torn.

people.name: Mar bar Rav Ashi
people.about: The Sage whose garment tore while he was walking.

people.name: Rav bar Shabba
people.about: A Sage who explained before Rav Kahana that human dignity overrides only rabbinic prohibitions.

terms.meaning: The principle that a person need not shame himself in public; the Gemara says it overrides rules made by the Sages, not those written in the Torah.
An area that is neither fully public nor private, where carrying on Shabbat is forbidden only by rabbinic law.

07.flag: The story is the second version of an incident whose first version, and the tear itself, come before the story begins, so it opens mid-scene.

08.note: Rabbi Beivai reported, in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, that a mule belonging to the household of Rabbi died and the Sages estimated its blood at a quarter-log. Rabbi Yitzhak bar Bisna objected with a testimony that a carcass's blood is pure, and with an incident told by Rabbi Yehoshua ben Beteira: wild donkeys were killed to feed the lions in the king's stadium, pilgrims waded in their blood up to the knees, and the Sages said nothing to them. Rabbi Beivai fell silent. When Rabbi Zerika asked why, he said his life was like the verse 'you shall have no assurance of your life', which Rabbi Hanin read as one who relies on a baker for bread; he relied on a baker. Rav Yosef later explained that Rabbi Yehuda, decisor for the Nasi's house, ruled by his own tradition.
08.why: The Gemara has been showing that the Sages' measures are exact, down to a hair; the mule's blood adds the quarter-log measure, and the objection asks whether a carcass's blood makes anyone impure at all.

people.name: Rabbi Beivai
people.about: The Sage who reports the incident of the mule and cannot answer the objection to it.

people.name: Rabbi Yitzhak bar Bisna
people.about: The Sage who objects that a carcass's blood is pure.

people.name: Rabbi Zerika
people.about: The Sage who asks Rabbi Beivai why he does not answer.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Beteira
people.about: An early Sage who told of pilgrims wading in donkeys' blood without the Sages objecting.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: The Sage who explains that Rabbi Yehuda ruled for the Nasi's house by his own tradition that such blood is impure.

terms.meaning: A small liquid measure, the minimum amount of blood that can make a person or thing ritually impure.
An animal that died without proper ritual slaughter; its flesh makes people ritually impure.
The head of the Jewish community in the Land of Israel; Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi held this office.

09.note: A host who had stolen money from his guests had lentils left on his mustache because he had not washed after eating. The guests went to his wife, said her husband had told them to ask her to return their money, and offered as proof that he had eaten lentils that day. She believed them and gave it back. In his anger, the husband divorced her.
09.why: Rav Dimi is teaching what can happen when people skip washing their hands before and after a meal; this is his case for washing after. Ravin then reports a harsher version in which the husband killed his wife.

terms.meaning: Washing the hands (and here the mouth) after a meal, as the Sages required.
Washing the hands before a meal.

09.flag: The Hebrew is a single line saying that neglecting the final waters led to a divorce; the incident itself appears only in the translator's explanation.

10.note: Levi visited the house of Yosef the bird hunter, where he was served a peacock's head cooked in milk, and he said nothing to them. When Levi came before Rabbi, Rabbi asked him why he had not excommunicated them. Levi answered that the town was the locale of Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira, and he thought Rabbi Yehuda might have taught them as Rabbi Yosei HaGelili did, that birds are excluded because they have no mother's milk.
10.why: The Gemara has just shown that Rabbi Yosei HaGelili left birds out of the ban on meat with milk, and that his own town ate poultry cooked in milk; Levi's silence shows a visitor respecting a town that follows its own teacher's ruling.

people.name: Levi
people.about: A Sage who is served a peacock's head in milk and stays silent.

people.name: Yosef the bird hunter
people.about: The host who served the dish.

people.name: Rabbi
people.about: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, who asks Levi why he did not excommunicate the household.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira
people.about: The Sage whose town it was, and whose ruling Levi did not want to overturn.

terms.meaning: To place someone under a ban that cuts him off from the community, a penalty for defying the Sages.
The Torah forbids cooking a kid in its mother's milk; the Sages debated whether this covers birds, which give no milk.

11.note: A butcher was suspected of selling the forbidden fat near the kidney as permitted intestinal fat. Rava penalized him by forbidding him to sell even nuts. Rav Pappa asked whether Rava was following the stricter view, in which case he should forbid even water and salt. Rava explained that the penalty was tied to the offense itself: the butcher had used nuts, which children love, to lure butchers' children into bringing him the forbidden fat, which he then sold as permitted.
11.why: The mishna has just set out a dispute: Rabbi Yehuda says one may buy nothing at all from a suspect seller, and Rabbi Shimon says only items connected to his offense are barred. Rava shows his ruling fits Rabbi Shimon.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The Sage who penalizes the butcher.

people.name: Rav Pappa
people.about: The Sage who questions which opinion Rava's penalty follows.

terms.meaning: Certain fats of cattle, sheep and goats, such as the fat around the kidneys, that the Torah forbids to be eaten, while other fat is permitted.

12.note: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar reported in the name of Rabbi Meir an incident about a woman who was married to a haver and would tie his phylacteries on his hand. Later she married a tax collector, and she would tie tax seals on his hand.
12.why: The Sages are debating whether the household of a haver who move into the home of someone less observant must formally take on the haver's commitments again; Rabbi Meir says they must, and the incident shows how fully a wife's practice follows her husband.

people.name: Rabbi Meir
people.about: The Sage who holds that even these people must take on the commitments, and in whose name the incident is told.

people.name: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar
people.about: The Sage who reports the incident.

terms.meaning: A member of a fellowship devoted to careful observance, especially of ritual purity and tithes.
Tefillin: leather boxes holding Torah verses, bound on the arm and head during prayer.
Marks or tokens a tax collector wore, here bound on the hand where phylacteries had been.

13.note: Rav Sheshet was troubled by a problem one night and solved it in the morning from a baraita. His attendant, Rav Idi, heard the solution from him and repeated it in the study hall without saying it was Rav Sheshet's. When Rav Sheshet heard, he was annoyed and said: the one who stung me, let him be stung by a scorpion.
13.why: The Gemara has found a contradiction over whether the meat of an animal tithe may be sold, which Rav Sheshet resolved. It explains his anger with Rav's teaching that David prayed for his words to be quoted in his name: a scholar quoted by name moves his lips in the grave.

people.name: Rav Sheshet
people.about: A Sage who solves a legal problem overnight and is angered when his answer is repeated without his name.

people.name: Rav Idi
people.about: Rav Sheshet's attendant, who repeats the solution in the study hall without crediting him.

people.name: David
people.about: King David, who according to Rav asked God that people repeat his teachings in his name after his death.

terms.meaning: A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna.
Every tenth newborn animal of the herd, which is consecrated; its meat may normally not be sold.
The place where the Sages and their students gathered to learn and debate.

14.note: The mother of Yirmatya vowed: I take upon myself to give my daughter's weight. She went up to Jerusalem and paid her daughter's weight in gold.
14.why: The mishna rules that one who vows his own weight gives that weight in the metal he named; the incident shows the same kind of vow made for a daughter and paid in gold.

people.name: The mother of Yirmatya
people.about: The woman who vowed her daughter's weight and paid it in gold.

terms.meaning: A spoken promise to give something to the Temple, which then becomes binding.
The fund of the Temple in Jerusalem, to which such donations were paid.

15.note: Rabbi Shimon told how, in the village of Pani, an old man asked him whether Rabbi Akiva really said that sprinkling the blood takes effect for sacrificial meat that has left the courtyard, and he answered yes. His colleagues in the Galilee objected: the meat is unfit, so how can the sprinkling work for it? When he brought this to Rabbi Akiva, Akiva said: my son, don't you agree? He pointed to two sin offerings, a lost one and its replacement, where sprinkling the blood of one frees the other's meat from the laws of misuse even though that other animal is unfit; all the more should the blood free its own meat.
15.why: Rabbi Akiva's comparison was cited and then limited by Rabbi Elazar to two animals slaughtered at once; right after this account, Reish Lakish says Akiva gave his student a misleading answer.

people.name: Rabbi Shimon
people.about: A student of Rabbi Akiva who brings him the question.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: The Sage whose ruling is questioned, and who defends it with a comparison.

people.name: A certain old man
people.about: The man in the village of Pani who first asks Rabbi Shimon about Rabbi Akiva's view.

terms.meaning: Applying an offering's blood to the altar, the act that completes a sacrifice.
The offense of using consecrated Temple property for personal benefit.
A sacrifice brought to atone for an unintentional sin.
A form of reasoning: if a rule holds in the weaker case, it surely holds in the stronger one.

16.note: Alexander of Macedon put ten questions to the Elders of the Negev: about distances, the order of creation (they declined to say whether light or darkness came first), who is wise, mighty and rich, how to live and how to die. When they said that even Satan is sometimes victorious, he threatened to execute them; they replied that falsehood does not suit a king, and he dressed them in purple and gold chains. Using their advice to cross the Mountains of Darkness, he reached a town of women, who served him bread of gold, and he wrote on its gate that he had learned sense from women. At a spring he guessed it flowed from the Garden of Eden. One version says he reached its gate, was refused, and was given an eyeball that outweighed all his gold, until it was covered with dust.
16.why: The Gemara has been explaining where the daily offerings were slaughtered by the position of the sun; Alexander's first question, answered from how hard it is to look at the sun at midday, ties the story to that discussion.

people.name: Alexander of Macedon
people.about: The king who questions the Elders of the Negev and goes on a campaign to Africa.

people.name: The Elders of the Negev
people.about: The Jewish Sages whom Alexander questions and who advise him.

people.name: The women of the town
people.about: The people of a town of women who talk Alexander out of fighting them.

terms.meaning: A dark mountain range that, the Elders said, blocked the way to Africa.
The garden of the first humans, here pictured as a real place whose gate only the righteous may enter.
In this text, a force that leads people to do what is clearly wrong.

17.note: A teaching of the Sages records an incident in which Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi gave a newly married virgin four nights, within the first twelve months of her marriage, during which blood after intercourse would be treated as blood of her torn hymen rather than menstrual blood. The text does not describe the case further.
17.why: Rav has just ruled that a grown woman is given only the first night; the Gemara raises this incident as an objection and begins asking at what age the bride was.

people.name: Rabbi
people.about: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, who grants the bride the four nights.

terms.meaning: Bleeding from first intercourse, which does not make a woman ritually impure, unlike menstrual blood.
A status that, for a menstruating woman, forbids marital relations until she purifies herself.

17.flag: The story is a one-line precedent and stops mid-sentence as the Gemara starts analyzing it.

18.note: Ravina arranged for his son to marry the daughter of Rav Hanina. Rav Hanina asked whether the marriage contract should set the wedding for Wednesday, and Ravina agreed. When Wednesday came, Ravina waited another week. Asked why, he cited Rava: a woman who accepts a marriage proposal must count seven clean days. Rav Hanina answered that Rava meant an adult woman who has seen blood, not a young girl who has not. Ravina replied that Rava had said so explicitly: the reason is that she desires her husband, and a young girl desires him too.
18.why: The Gemara has just cited Rava's ruling that a woman who accepts a proposal must count seven clean days; this incident shows the ruling put into practice and extends it to a girl who has not yet menstruated.

people.name: Ravina
people.about: The father of the groom, who delays the wedding a week.

people.name: Rav Hanina
people.about: The father of the bride, who questions the delay.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The Sage whose ruling Ravina follows.

terms.meaning: The ketuba, the document a groom gives his bride setting out his obligations, here also fixing the wedding date.
Seven days without any flow of blood, after which a woman immerses in a ritual bath and may resume marital relations.
